# What extant finds, measured

extant checks whether the claims in a project's documentation are still true,
against git and the filesystem. It never judges whether a value is CORRECT,
only whether something the documentation names still exists or still holds: a
commit that no longer resolves, a file a link points at, a heading an anchor
expects, a version claimed as released with no such tag. A `finding` below is
one such claim that no longer holds. Numbers and dates are deliberately out of
scope, because nothing can check them.

This is what that finds when it is pointed at other people's repositories.
Every figure is computed from recorded sweeps rather than from a demonstration,
and none of it is typed by hand: the report is rendered from the measurements,
so a stale number fails a check instead of surviving in prose. The last section
says exactly which check runs where, and what is still left to human
discipline.

## The corpora

| corpus | repositories | documents | findings | ordinary | reporting |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| bench | 50 | 37,073 | 56,084 | 5,691 (10.1%) | 39 |
| heldout | 20 | 12,579 | 206 | 185 (89.8%) | 16 |
| niche | 38 | 13,562 | 5,142 | 4,943 (96.1%) | 25 |
| agent | 17 | 28,815 | 729 | 605 (83.0%) | 14 |

Counted over the swept population, which is the same population the precision
figures use. Across all four that is 122 distinct repositories; the tiers share
3, so the rows above do not simply add up.

`ordinary` is what is left once the strata separate out changelogs, vendored
trees, generated API references and per-release documentation snapshots. It is
the half a reader would act on, and on the benchmark it is a small fraction of
the total:

| stratum | findings |
|:---|---:|
| version-snapshot | 39,701 |
| ordinary | 5,691 |
| historical-record | 4,764 |
| vendored | 4,198 |
| generated | 1,730 |

So 50,393 of 56,084 benchmark findings sit in a kind of tree nobody would act
on. They are labelled rather than hidden, and the ordinary count is what the
summary leads with.

Concentration is reported rather than left to be discovered: the largest single
contributor to the benchmark's ordinary findings is `tensorflow/tensorflow`, at
1,593 of them (28.0%).

## The reserve

**32 repositories have never been swept.** They are held back so a rule change
can be measured against ground it was not tuned on, and opening them requires a
stated reason that is printed with the results.

| corpus | in manifest | reserved | swept | never swept |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| agent | 17 | 0 | 17 | 0 |
| bench | 50 | 11 | 50 | 0 |
| heldout | 40 | 20 | 20 | 20 |
| niche | 50 | 12 | 38 | 12 |

Two different things wear the word. 11 benchmark repositories are flagged
reserve but were swept, and are only withheld from tuning decisions. Just the
32 never-swept ones can answer whether a rule fires on ground nobody has looked
at, so they are counted apart instead of summed.

## What a default install actually checks

A survey of the whole repository is not what an adopter gets. The installer
configures the one or two documents it can name with confidence, and on the
benchmark that gate covers **7 of the 5,691 ordinary findings** the survey
sees - 5 of 50 repositories report anything at all under it. The rest would
exit 0 forever, which is a validator teaching its adopters it has nothing to
say.

Counted across every stratum rather than ordinary alone it is 12 of 56,084,
which is the same story told about a larger pile.

The cause is document SELECTION rather than the rules, so the fix is a wider
document set. Each policy below was measured over the same sweep; `pinned
paths` is the standing liability each one accepts, because a pinned document
that later moves becomes a finding until somebody edits the config:

| policy | findings gated | ordinary | paths pinned | repositories reporting |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `installed` | 12 | 7 | 66 | 5 |
| `root` | 73 | 21 | 260 | 17 |
| `root+docs` | 221 | 169 | 522 | 21 |
| `root+docs-ord` | 169 | 169 | 490 | 15 |
| `docs2-ord` | 497 | 497 | 1,978 | 22 |
| `docs3-ord` | 1,123 | 1,123 | 3,305 | 24 |
| `docs4-ord` | 1,139 | 1,139 | 5,525 | 24 |
| `ordinary` | 5,691 | 5,691 | 25,189 | 39 |

Two of those rows are worth reading against each other. `root` gates 73
findings against `installed`'s 12 and is still the worse policy: per path it
pins, it returns 0.081 ordinary findings against 0.106. Most of what it
collects is `CHANGELOG.md`, which is why every widened policy here is
restricted to the ordinary stratum - the restriction is the feature rather than
a refinement of it.

And a fourth level is a cliff rather than a slope: 16 more findings for 2,220
more pinned paths. That is where the default depth stops.

The `installed` row counts only the repositories the installer agreed to
configure. Everywhere it refused to write a configuration at all, the policy
has no answer rather than an answer of zero: bench (5 of 50); heldout (20 of
20); niche (38 of 38); agent (17 of 17). Those repositories were never asked
the question, which is a different thing from being asked and reporting
nothing, and folding them in as zeroes would understate the gate while looking
like a measurement.

## Precision

Against a hand-labelled sample of 1,402 findings, pooled precision is
**99.29%** raw and 99.52% reweighted by stratum.

Precision of exactly the findings a wider gate would newly FAIL a build on is
measured separately, because the cost of being wrong changes character once a
survey line becomes a failing build. Each row names the selection policy it was
measured under; they are not interchangeable.

| corpus | policy | judged | resolve under some reading | precision |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| bench | `docs3-ord` | 1,125 | 14 | 98.8% |
| bench | `root+docs-ord` | 168 | 1 | 99.4% |
| heldout | `docs3-ord` | 33 | 0 | 100.0% |
| niche | `docs3-ord` | 4,595 | 20 | 99.6% |

A finding counts against precision if its citation resolves under ANY reading a
real one could legitimately have: case-folded, a missing extension, a directory
index, a schemeless URL. That is deliberately harsher than re-running the rule,
which would re-ask the rule's own question and agree with itself.

## SHA citations, and the answer that inverted the question

This section counts a DIFFERENT set of repositories from the tables above, and
the difference is not an error: asking git whether a cited commit exists needs
full history, so it was run over the corpora that were cloned with it rather
than over the shallow ones. That is 75 distinct repositories from 88 clones, 13
of them held twice and de-duplicated in favour of the deeper copy.

Across those, documentation cites 20,428 commit SHAs, 14,843 of them distinct.

| what git says | citations |
|:---|---:|
| live | 11,781 |
| absent | 8,550 |
| hex-collision | 54 |
| unreachable | 43 |

41.9% of cited SHAs do not resolve, and the obvious reading is that
documentation invents them. Asked properly on a held-out agent-written project,
it answered the other way: every dead SHA there appeared in the rewrite map a
history rewrite had left behind. They were not invented, they were rewritten,
and the evidence was on disk the whole time. A further 54 are hex collisions
that were never commit citations at all.

## The agent pilot that decided nothing

A pilot asked whether an agent given a validator verifies claims more reliably
than one without: 6 sessions across 3 arms, 7 planted defects each.

| arm | sessions | detected | false negatives | false alarms |
|:---|---:|:---|:---|:---|
| A | 2 | 7 | 0 | 3, 4 |
| B | 2 | 7 | 0 | 1, 4 |
| C | 2 | 7 | 0 | 4, 5 |

**Every arm detected 7 of 7, with no false negatives anywhere.** That is not a
finding that the arms are equal - it is a fixture that cannot tell them apart.
The pilot is reported as saturated and deciding nothing, because publishing the
scores without that sentence would read as a result about agents.

## What changed since these figures were first published

An earlier write-up recorded 54,790 benchmark findings (4,429 ordinary). The
current figure is 56,084 (5,691), a change of +1,294. It is the sum of two
changes made in this order, and each is stated with its cause rather than left
for a reader to tell a correction from a mistake.

**One narrowing removed findings.** A schemeless URL such as
`www.example.com/x` was being read as a relative path and reported as a dead
link.

| corpus | before | after | removed | added |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| bench | 54,790 | 54,772 | 18 | 0 |
| heldout | 204 | 200 | 4 | 0 |
| niche | 5,159 | 5,136 | 23 | 0 |

`added` is a set difference rather than a subtraction of totals, so it would
show a narrowing that removed real findings and invented new ones. It reports
0.

**Two widening passes, and one review, added findings.** Four rules read shapes
they had not read - a reference-style link definition, the `href` and `src` of
raw HTML, a line range to its end, both ends of a dotted commit range, a link
carrying a title and an angle-bracketed destination - and two misreads were
corrected on the way: an angle-bracketed URL cut at a parenthesis and reported
as a file, and a link to `.` reported as a missing one. The recordings the
narrowing was published from were taken with the tool as it then was, so the
table holds everything since, not the widenings alone.

| corpus | before | after | removed | added | added, ordinary | of which read |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| agent | 712 | 729 | 0 | 17 | 17 | 17 |
| bench | 54,772 | 56,084 | 18 | 1,326 | 1,282 | 295 |
| heldout | 200 | 206 | 1 | 7 | 7 | 7 |
| niche | 5,136 | 5,142 | 6 | 12 | 3 | 12 |

Across the four: 1,362 added, 1,309 of them ordinary, and 25 removed - the
misreads corrected, and the findings a correction respelled. `of which read` is
computed, not claimed: each addition in a repository the widenings were
measured on is matched against the rows those passes read one by one before
shipping, and 331 of the 333 match. The rest are the review's, not a
widening's. The readings are in the design record, with the proposals refused
on them.

The other 1,029 on bench sat in its reserve when the widenings were measured,
1,019 of them in tensorflow/tensorflow, and no widening pass read them: the
reserve is held for exactly that later evaluation, and reading it spends it.

5 of those repositories had their reserve opened and spent on 2026-09-13, so
the additions could be read rather than published unjudged. None of them is
unseen ground for anything measured after that date, and the manifest says so.
What the reading found, repository by repository:

**tensorflow/tensorflow**, 1,019 read: 1,003 routes in an undetected DevSite
tree, each resolving once .md is appended; 15 routes in a generated all_symbols
index written one directory too shallow, in the same tree; 1 real broken image
in a vendored README under third_party/xla. The known undetected-generator
class, multiplied by the raw-HTML arm: no new false-positive shape, and one
real finding, labelled vendored.

**rust-lang/rust**, 15 read: 11 rustdoc intra-doc links in markdown that a
#[doc = include_str!] pulls into rustdoc, not files; 1 page an mdBook three
levels down serves from README.md under the name index.md; 1 page the
unstable-book generator writes at build time; 1 real: a dead link in clippy's
changelog, labelled historical-record; 1 real: a rustc-dev-guide page,
generic_arguments.md, that no longer exists. Thirteen false in three classes
and two real. The eleven rustdoc links are refused by the tool since 2026-09-14
and are not in these figures, so the table shows the four that remain. A
sixteenth, a definition-shaped changelog line CommonMark reads as a paragraph,
was a scanner defect; it was fixed and the recordings taken again.

**microsoft/vscode**, 5 read: 5 titled image links in test fixtures, the
copilot scenario examples and a colorize fixture. All five fixtures, which
exclude_paths is for.

**vercel/next.js**, 2 read: 2 rustdoc intra-doc links in markdown that a #[doc
= include_str!] pulls into rustdoc, not files. Both false, the rustdoc class,
refused by the tool since 2026-09-14 and not in these figures.

**denoland/deno**, 1 read: 1 HTML link in an npm package's README copied into
bench test data without its docs directory. Test data, which exclude_paths is
for.

The precision figures were sampled and labelled from the recordings these
replaced, so they cover none of the additions; the additions that were read
were read in full rather than sampled.

## How this file is kept honest

It is generated, not written. The figures are computed from recorded sweeps,
and the prose above is rendered from them, so a number cannot be edited here
without the render stopping to match.

Checking that splits in two, because the evidence for each half lives somewhere
different:

| what could go wrong | what catches it | where it runs |
|:---|:---|:---|
| this file edited by hand, or left behind when the figures moved | `tests/test_corpus_report.py` re-renders `CORPUS-figures.json` and requires it to reproduce this file | every test run, including CI |
| the figures no longer match the corpus they came from | `corpus_report.py --check` | only where the corpus is, which is far too large to commit |

```sh
python -m pytest tests/test_corpus_report.py  # the committed pair agree
python corpus_report.py --check CORPUS.md     # figures match the corpus
python corpus_report.py --write CORPUS.md     # rewrite both files
```

Neither half is sufficient alone, and the second cannot run in CI. That is a
weaker guarantee than a single check would be; it is the strongest one
available without committing the corpus, and saying which half runs where
seemed better than implying both always do.

The generator reads only recorded measurement output. It never sweeps, clones,
or asks git anything, so a figure that is not in the data cannot appear here.
